description_full: Applied Materials, Inc. provides materials engineering solutions, equipment, services, and software to the semiconductor and related industries in the United States, China, Korea, Taiwan, Japan, Southeast Asia, Europe, and internationally. The company operates through Semiconductor Systems and Applied Global Services (AGS) segments. The Semiconductor Systems segment includes semiconductor capital equipment to enable materials engineering steps, including etch, rapid thermal processing, deposition, chemical mechanical planarization, metrology and inspection, wafer packaging, and ion implantation. The AGS segment offers integrated solutions to optimize equipment and fab performance and productivity comprising spares, upgrades, services, and 200 millimeter and other equipment and factory automation software for semiconductor and other products. It serves manufacturers of semiconductor wafers and chips, and other electronic devices. Applied Materials, Inc. was incorporated in 1967 and is headquartered in Santa Clara, California.

financial_summary: Applied Materials, Inc. is a mega-cap technology business with a $294.0B market cap on $28.4B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +3% over the past three years and +11% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory. Operating margins are expanding by +2.3pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 45% against a 12% cost of capital — a 33-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, with gross margins sitting at 44%.

The business throws off $5.7B in free cash flow — roughly 20 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.14× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 31× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield of 2.0% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 29% operating margin runs 22pp above the Technology median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.25x).
It accounts for 0.6% of sector revenue and 0.8% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-2.6% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 533 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 109% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 29% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 50% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 64% and a beta of 1.54, it amplifies market moves.
Liquidity is deep, with about $2.9B traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 44% in the 2020 crash, 55% in the 2022 bear market and 62% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $218 (margin of safety -70%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 48%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $130 to $368 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Technology peers: EV/EBITDA 25.1 vs 17.1 and P/FCF 51.6 vs 26.1 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 155% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 1.9% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 2.8% (vs the 8% bar).
The 36 covering analysts target $608 on average, 64% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 45% clears the cost of capital of 11.8% by 33pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.59).
It runs a 44% gross margin and converts 20% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 1.14x.
ROE of 34% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.8x equity multiplier).
It spends 12.6% of revenue on R&D and 2.4% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $2.0B (1% of market cap).
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 15.2, in the safe zone).
Working capital ties up about 165 days of sales, a drag on cash generation.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 3.2% over 3 years, 10.5% over 5 years and 11.4% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 25%).
At current returns, reinvesting 31% of profits supports about 14.1% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 11.0% a year over five years.
Capex runs 5.2x depreciation (8.0% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.3%), and institutions hold 84%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (36 sales, net $169.0M sold).
It returns 2.0% a year to shareholders (1.6% in buybacks and 0.6% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 2.8% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 20 consecutive years, raising it 12.0% a year over the last five.
people: CEO pay is $2.7M, and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
